title: tensorrt-triton-custom-kernel-integration-experiments-draft
content:
Summary:

This is a working write-up of experiments we ran to evaluate integration options for high-performance inference: Triton+TensorRT (out-of-the-box Triton TRT backend), direct TensorRT integration (custom runtime harness using serialized engines), and a small set of hand-written custom CUDA kernels for attention / KV-cache hotspots. Goal is to capture quantitative tradeoffs (latency/throughput/95p tail), engineering surface area (build/CI/deploy complexity), and operational implications for KV cache and scheduling.

Context and goals:
- Primary goal: reduce p50/p95 latency and cost-per-token for autoregressive decoding workloads while preserving reliability and compatibility with our rollout tooling.
- Secondary: measure how integration choices affect dynamic batching, variable sequence lengths, and KV-cache semantics.
- Models tested: Llama2-13B (fp16/4-bit quant), Llama-70B (fp16 only), and a smaller 7B test model used for fast iteration.
- Hardware: A100-80GB (pinned test cluster), and T4 for smaller config checks.
- Workloads: single-request low-latency (seq_len=256, batch=1), bursty traffic (many small concurrent requests), and throughput-mode long sequences (seq_len=2048, batch aggregated).

Experiments run (high level):
1) Triton TRT backend (model repository, TRT optimization via ONNX->TRT inside Triton).
   - default Triton batching + dynamic batching profiles enabled.
   - measured engine build time inside Triton and memory behavior.
2) Direct TensorRT integration (we manage engine build, serialization, and a tiny runtime wrapper).
   - use CUDA graph warmup and persistent execution contexts.
   - engine rebuilt per max sequence/profile; used explicit optimization profiles for 128/256/512/2048.
3) Custom kernels for attention and KV candidates (hand-tuned fused attention, custom KV packing).
   - integrated into our runtime as an alternate op path behind a feature flag.
   - used for larger models where attention dominates compute.

Metrics captured:
- p50/p90/p95 latency (ms) for token step (next-token), and end-to-end request latency for short prompts.
- Throughput (tokens/sec) under steady-state generation for long sequences.
- GPU memory footprint and fragmentation (peak alloc, reserved).
- Engine build time / cold-start for TRT.
- Operational metrics: frequency of fallback events, error surface (OOMs, unsupported op errors).

Key quantitative findings (representative numbers from runs on A100):
- TensorRT (direct) vs Triton-TRT:
  - Direct TensorRT gave ~1.6-1.9x throughput improvement over Triton-TRT for steady-state long sequences (Llama2-13B, fp16), mainly due to fewer orchestration overheads and our ability to pre-warm CUDA graphs.
  - Triton-TRT p95 latency was ~15-25% higher than direct TRT for small batches (batch=1) because Triton introduces additional request/response plumbing and model-repository checks.
  - Triton advantages: easier model lifecycle (hot-swap), built-in batching, and standard metrics integration.
- Custom kernels:
  - When replacing attention with our fused kernel + optimized KV layout we observed up to 2.3-2.6x throughput compared to Triton-TRT and ~1.2-1.4x over direct TensorRT for the largest models (Llama-70B) in fp16 runs.
  - For shorter sequences/custom batch shapes the gains reduced to ~1.1-1.2x since kernel launch overheads and memory copies start to dominate.
- Quantization and INT8:
  - INT8+calibration on TensorRT gave ~1.8x token throughput vs fp16 for 13B, but quality regressions were model/prompt-dependent. Calibration time and dataset sensitivity are non-trivial operational costs.

Observations and tradeoffs:
1) Build-time and deployment complexity:
   - Triton-TRT: easiest to operate. We can push an ONNX + Triton config and let Triton manage engine builds. However, in-cluster engine builds are expensive and cause jitter on shared GPU pools unless isolated.
   - Direct TensorRT: more control over engine builds (we pre-build offline and store artifacts). This reduces runtime jitter but requires us to maintain engine artifact metadata (profile -> engine mapping) and handle compatibility across driver/runtime versions.
   - Custom kernels: highest maintenance. Kernels need to be validated across CUDA/driver versions and require CI on multiple GPU types. However, they can capture algorithmic optimizations not exposed by TRT.

2) Dynamic shapes and batching:
   - Triton handles dynamic batching and multiple optimization profiles gracefully. Dynamic batching in Triton is convenient but can increase p95 for low-latency requests unless configured with tight max-delay thresholds.
   - TensorRT requires explicit optimization profiles. Supporting a wide range of shapes forces many engines or aggressive profile ranges with less optimal kernels. We found 4-5 profiles (128/256/512/1024/2048) gives a good coverage/engine-count tradeoff.
   - Custom kernels can be written to handle variable sequence lengths efficiently (e.g., windowed attention), but that adds code complexity.

3) KV cache semantics and memory tradeoffs:
   - Shared vs per-request KV: sharing caches across sessions (or across requests from the same user) reduces recomputation but complicates isolation and eviction policies.
   - Triton model instances: we used multiple model instances pinned to GPUs to preserve per-session KV in local GPU memory; this reduced cross-instance copying but increased memory footprint and decreased consolidation efficiency.
   - For direct TRT we implemented a sharded KV-cache manager: part of KV stays on-GPU pinned memory, part spills to host if memory pressure. This gave better consolidation and higher overall throughput under bursty workloads, but increased latency variance for spill events.

4) Cold-starts and engine build time:
   - Triton sometimes triggered engine builds on first inference which caused high latency spikes. Mitigation: pre-warm with representative inputs during deployment and ensure build containers have isolated GPUs or do offline builds.
   - Direct TRT with serialized engines avoids in-cluster builds and gave more predictable tail latency.

5) Reliability and fallback behavior:
   - Triton provides a mature platform-level mechanism for model fallback and multi-version serving. If a Triton TRT engine build fails it reports cleanly and you can fall back to an alternative.
   - Direct TRT needs our runtime to manage fallbacks explicitly; we added a lightweight orchestrator to route to a fallback engine (e.g., fp16->fp32) on error.

Engineering cost estimates (rough):
- Triton-backed approach: low engineering effort to get to production; ops costs for capacity isolation (to avoid in-cluster engine build OOMs).
- Direct TensorRT: moderate engineering cost (artifact management, warmup pipelines, per-profile engine management), operational benefit of predictable latency.
- Custom kernels: high ongoing maintenance cost. Worth it only if we need sustained 20-40%+ perf delta that translates directly to significant cost savings.

Recommendations (current):
1) Short term (MVP): use Triton-TRT for self-serve hosted tiers where operator friction should be minimal. Add pre-build/offline engine pipeline to avoid in-cluster builds on release.
2) Mid term (cost-sensitive customers / Dedicated): offer a direct-TensorRT deployment path for Dedicated clusters with offline prebuilt engines + engine artifact manager + warmup service. This provides best operational predictability and lower tail latency.
3) Long term (R&D): continue targeted custom-kernel work for attention/KV hotspot ops, but gate these behind opt-in feature flags and focus on maintainability (shared library, CI across GPU families). Consider open-sourcing less critical kernel pieces to externalize maintenance.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need a production plan for INT8 calibration dataset management and A/B quality evaluation tooling (eval suites tied to customer prompts).
- Measure cross-driver/runtime compatibility breaking rate for serialized TRT engines across our fleet images (we saw 2-3% mismatches in pilot). Add CI to detect these early.
- Explore hybrid scheduling: Triton for control-plane features (rollouts, metrics) + direct TRT execution path behind the scenes for latency-critical routes. Prototype a light-weight shim.

Notes / links:
- Experimental scripts and raw outputs are in the linked PR and ENG-2147 ticket.
- Bench harness used: local harness that simulates token-step workloads with realistic prompt distribution (see github PR).

Appendix (quick checklist for next runs):
- [ ] Add T4-family runs for cost-sensitive smaller instances.
- [ ] Run full A/B eval for INT8 models on a held-out eval set.
- [ ] Add CI job to validate serialized TRT artifacts across driver versions.
- [ ] Build warmup service that runs representative traces during deploy.

Notes-to-self (informal):
- We should capture metadata mapping: model-version -> set of engine files -> required CUDA/driver. Might store as small manifest in bucket keyed by image-version.
- Consider a thin orchestrator layer that lets Triton own the control-plane, but delegates heavy-path inference to our direct TRT runtime when a flag is set. Could be the fastest path to combine Triton ops ergonomics with direct perf.

End of draft.
